headline: GH after your
punch: Bones stop lengthening. They keep changing.

headline: Is it pointless after fusion?
body: So the usual assumption is that growth hormone becomes irrelevant to your skeleton the moment your growth plates fuse. No plate, no lengthening, nothing left to gain, stop wasting your money. | The lengthening half of that is completely correct. The nothing-left-to-gain half is not, and the reason is that bone grows along two different axes with two different deadlines, and almost everyone only tracks one of them.
punch: Bones stop getting longer. They do not stop changing.

headline: So what keeps growing?
body: Length comes from the growth plate, through endochondral ossification, and that process has a hard end date when the plate fuses. That is the one everyone measures. | **Width** comes from the *periosteum*, the layer wrapped around the outside of the shaft, which lays new bone directly onto the surface. That process runs on osteoblasts, osteoblasts carry GH receptors, and it has no closing date at all.
punch: Length has a deadline. Width does not.

headline: Delete the GH receptor
body: The cleanest way to ask whether GH matters for that second process is to remove the receptor and look. Mice with the GH receptor deleted have **reduced femoral width and low cortical bone mass**, with a very low mineral apposition rate at 4 weeks of age. | Their osteoblast surface area is reduced too, which is consistent with impaired osteoblast proliferation. What this means is that with no GH signal the bone comes out narrower, independent of anything happening at the plate.

headline: Give rats GH instead
body: Run the experiment in the other direction and you get the mirror image. GH **induces subperiosteal bone formation associated with increased mechanical strength**, meaning new bone laid onto the outer surface of the shaft and a measurably stronger bone as a result. | Svensson's secretagogue work found the same shape of answer from a different angle: bone mineral content rose while volumetric density was unchanged. The bones got bigger rather than denser.

headline: Fracture incidence
body: All of that is mechanism, so here is the outcome that matters. GH replacement therapy stimulates bone turnover, improves bone mass during childhood and adolescence, and **decreases fracture incidence by 3 or 4 fold**. | That is a hard clinical endpoint, not a surrogate marker like a density scan or a blood result. Whether a bone breaks is the thing bone density is a proxy for, and this is measuring it directly.

headline: Still IGF-1 underneath
body: The mediator is still IGF-1. Reduced cortical bone formation in GH receptor knockout mice **can be restored with IGF-1 treatment**, which places IGF-1 downstream here just as it is at the growth plate. | But the signalling route differs. These bone anabolic actions **do not require STAT5**: deleting both STAT5a and STAT5b left cortical thickness and mineral apposition rate unaffected. So it is the same messenger travelling by a different road than the liver one.
punch: A different pathway from the liver one.

headline: What to measure instead
body: After fusion, GH stops being a height drug and continues as a bone drug. Width, cortical mass and fracture risk are all still live outcomes, and all three have data behind them. | Which means the right thing to judge it on changes the moment your plates close, and almost nobody changes what they measure. They keep checking height, see nothing, and conclude nothing is happening.
punch: ==Stop measuring height. Start measuring the bone.==
